title: Umbraco.Cms: Open Redirect Vulnerability in Surface Controllers

scenario.summary: Open Redirect (GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-2qjj-h6wp-c7h7) in Umbraco.Cms.
preconditions: A redirect/return-URL parameter accepts an arbitrary external destination without validation

process.action: Find redirect-driving parameters (redirect_uri, next, return_to, url)
process.expected_observation: Parameter controls the Location header or client-side redirect

process.action: Set the parameter to an external domain and observe the response
process.expected_observation: 302/JS redirect points to the attacker-controlled external domain

process.action: Bypass any host validation (protocol-relative URLs, backslash tricks, allow-listed-domain-as-prefix tricks)
process.expected_observation: Redirect succeeds despite a naive allow-list check

process.action: Chain with a phishing or OAuth token-leak scenario to demonstrate real impact
process.expected_observation: Sensitive token/parameter is leaked to the external domain via the referrer or redirect chain

impact: Phishing via a trusted domain's redirect, increasing credibility of the attack
OAuth/SSO token leakage when chained with authorization flows
remediation: Validate redirect destinations against a strict allow-list of internal paths/domains
Avoid accepting full URLs from user input for redirect purposes; use indirect reference IDs

title: Winter: Authenticated backend users can bypass Users controller permission checks

scenario.summary: Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) (GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-j5jq-cr68-v2xx) in winter/wn-backend-module.
preconditions: Application exposes object identifiers (numeric IDs, UUIDs, usernames, file paths) in URLs, API params, or request bodies
Two accounts of the same privilege level are available for differential testing
Access control checks are applied inconsistently across endpoints

process.action: Map every endpoint that accepts an object identifier
process.expected_observation: List of endpoints with id-like parameters (order_id, user_id, file, uuid)

process.action: Record a baseline request/response as user A for an object A owns
process.expected_observation: 200 response containing user A's own object data

process.action: Replay the same request using user B's session/token but referencing object A's identifier
process.expected_observation: If access control is broken, the response returns user A's object data to user B

process.action: Enumerate adjacent identifiers (sequential IDs, predictable UUIDs) to confirm the issue is systemic, not a one-off
process.expected_observation: Multiple unrelated objects accessible across the ID space

process.action: Test write/delete operations (not just read) on the same identifier pattern
process.expected_observation: Unauthorized modification or deletion succeeds

impact: Unauthorized read access to other users' private data
Unauthorized modification or deletion of other users' resources
Potential account takeover if the exposed object includes credentials or session tokens
remediation: Enforce server-side ownership/authorization checks on every object access, not just at the UI layer
Use indirect, non-guessable references (per-user mapping tokens) instead of raw sequential IDs where feasible
Add automated authorization tests to CI that assert cross-account access is denied

preconditions: Application exposes object identifiers (numeric IDs, UUIDs, usernames, file paths) in URLs, API params, or request bodies
Two accounts of the same privilege level are available for differential testing
Access control checks are applied inconsistently across endpoints

process.action: Map every endpoint that accepts an object identifier
process.expected_observation: List of endpoints with id-like parameters (order_id, user_id, file, uuid)

process.action: Record a baseline request/response as user A for an object A owns
process.expected_observation: 200 response containing user A's own object data

process.action: Replay the same request using user B's session/token but referencing object A's identifier
process.expected_observation: If access control is broken, the response returns user A's object data to user B

process.action: Enumerate adjacent identifiers (sequential IDs, predictable UUIDs) to confirm the issue is systemic, not a one-off
process.expected_observation: Multiple unrelated objects accessible across the ID space

process.action: Test write/delete operations (not just read) on the same identifier pattern
process.expected_observation: Unauthorized modification or deletion succeeds

impact: Unauthorized read access to other users' private data
Unauthorized modification or deletion of other users' resources
Potential account takeover if the exposed object includes credentials or session tokens
remediation: Enforce server-side ownership/authorization checks on every object access, not just at the UI layer
Use indirect, non-guessable references (per-user mapping tokens) instead of raw sequential IDs where feasible
Add automated authorization tests to CI that assert cross-account access is denied

process.action: Identify price-dependent logic sourced from a single spot price

process.action: Determine that the underlying liquidity pool is manipulable within one transaction relative to available capital
process.expected_observation: Pool depth is small enough that a large but obtainable swap meaningfully moves the reported price

process.action: Borrow large capital (typically via flash loan) and swap to skew the pool's reported price
process.expected_observation: Oracle-reported price is now significantly distorted from the true market price

process.action: Exploit the skewed price within the same transaction (e.g. borrow against inflated collateral, or buy underpriced assets), then repay the loan
process.expected_observation: Attacker extracts value inconsistent with the true market price before the price reverts

impact: Undercollateralized loans drained from lending protocols
Arbitrage-free drains of AMM pools or vaults
Cascading liquidation failures across dependent protocols
remediation: Use time-weighted average price (TWAP) oracles or decentralized oracle networks (e.g. Chainlink) instead of single-block spot prices
Require multi-block price observation before acting on price-sensitive logic

title: Sylius: Cart FormComponent allows modification or deletion of an already-completed order

scenario.summary: Reentrancy (GitHub Security Advisory GHSA-5597-7rmh-97q5) in sylius/sylius.
preconditions: A contract makes an external call (e.g. .call, .send, .transfer to an untrusted address) before updating its own state (checks-effects-interactions violated)

process.action: Identify external calls that precede state updates in the target contract
process.expected_observation: An external call to msg.sender or an arbitrary address occurs before balance/state variables are updated

process.action: Confirm the callee can execute arbitrary code on receipt and no reentrancy guard is present
process.expected_observation: No nonReentrant modifier or equivalent guard protects the vulnerable function

process.action: Deploy an attacker contract whose fallback/receive function re-calls the vulnerable function
process.expected_observation: Nested recursive calls succeed before the first call's state update completes

process.action: Trigger repeated recursive withdrawal before the balance is zeroed, draining funds
process.expected_observation: Contract balance drained beyond the attacker's legitimate entitlement

impact: Complete drain of contract funds
Corruption of internal accounting state
Historically catastrophic impact (The DAO hack, 2016, ~$60M)
remediation: Follow the checks-effects-interactions pattern: update state before making external calls
Use a reentrancy guard (e.g. OpenZeppelin's ReentrancyGuard / nonReentrant modifier)
Prefer pull-over-push payment patterns
Limit gas forwarded on external calls where appropriate

impact: Denial of service via crashing application logic

remediation: Use Object.create(null) or Map for user-controlled key/value storage instead of plain objects

preconditions: JavaScript code merges/clones user-controlled objects using a recursive merge that does not block __proto__/constructor.prototype keys

process.action: Identify client- or server-side JS code paths that merge user input into an object (deep merge, clone, JSON parse into config)
process.expected_observation: Recursive merge/assign function reachable with attacker-controlled keys

process.action: Submit a payload with a __proto__ or constructor.prototype key to attempt polluting Object.prototype
process.expected_observation: A new property appears on all objects (e.g. {}.polluted === 'yes')

process.action: Identify a gadget that consumes the polluted property in a security-sensitive way (e.g. an isAdmin default, template rendering flag)
process.expected_observation: Application behavior changes based on the polluted global property

process.action: Chain the pollution with the identified gadget to achieve a concrete impact (privilege escalation, XSS, DoS)
process.expected_observation: Concrete security impact (e.g. unauthorized admin UI rendered) confirmed

impact: Denial of service via crashing application logic
Privilege escalation or XSS when a polluted property is consumed by a security-relevant gadget
remediation: Use Object.create(null) or Map for user-controlled key/value storage instead of plain objects
Use merge/clone libraries that explicitly block __proto__, constructor, and prototype keys
Freeze Object.prototype in sensitive contexts where feasible

preconditions: The server fetches a URL/resource on behalf of the user (webhooks, image/PDF fetchers, URL preview, import-from-URL features)

process.action: Find features where the server fetches a remote resource based on user input

process.action: Attempt to bypass any allow-list/deny-list filtering (DNS rebinding, redirects, alternate IP encodings)

process.action: Extract sensitive data reachable only from the server's network position (cloud credentials, internal admin panels)

impact: Access to internal-only services and admin interfaces not exposed externally
Cloud credential theft via instance metadata services, often leading to full cloud account compromise

Use a dedicated proxy for outbound fetches with strict egress controls
